PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 90 — Lesson 114: Diabetic Foot Ulcer, Infection & Limb Preservation

FNP-level goal: Treat a diabetes-related foot problem as an interaction among neuropathy, pressure, deformity, ischemia, skin breakdown, and infection; recognize limb- and life-threatening presentations; and coordinate prevention, offloading, wound care, vascular assessment, glycemic management, and specialty referral without reducing the visit to an antibiotic decision.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how loss of protective sensation, foot deformity, repetitive pressure, peripheral artery disease, delayed healing, and infection lead to ulceration and amputation risk.
  • Perform and document a comprehensive diabetes foot assessment, including skin, nails, deformity, sensation, pulses, footwear, ulcer history, and current symptoms.
  • Assess an ulcer for depth, tissue, drainage, infection, ischemia, foreign body, osteomyelitis risk, and need for offloading or urgent surgical or vascular evaluation.
  • Distinguish colonization from clinical infection and understand why an infected diabetes-related foot requires severity assessment and often interdisciplinary care.
  • Provide a longitudinal prevention plan that protects feet between visits and closes referral loops for podiatry, wound care, vascular care, surgery, and diabetes management.

Part 1 — The Diabetic Foot Is a Systems Problem

A plantar ulcer rarely begins with one dramatic injury. Distal symmetric neuropathy reduces pain and protective sensation. Motor changes and deformity create focal high-pressure points. Autonomic changes can dry and crack skin. Peripheral artery disease reduces tissue perfusion and healing reserve. Hyperglycemia, kidney disease, smoking, poor vision, limited mobility, inadequate footwear, and social barriers can add risk. A patient may walk on a foreign body, blister, callus, or ulcer without pain until infection or tissue loss becomes advanced.

That is why a painless ulcer is not a mild ulcer. Pain is an unreliable severity marker in neuropathic feet. The FNP must examine rather than wait for symptoms, and must look beyond the wound to pressure, perfusion, infection, function, shoes, support, and ability to complete the plan.

Part 2 — Prevention Starts With Risk Stratification

All people with diabetes need periodic foot assessment; those with sensory loss, peripheral artery disease, deformity, prior ulcer or amputation, kidney failure, smoking, or Charcot history need more frequent surveillance and specialty support. A focused history includes burning, numbness, tingling, loss of balance, claudication, rest pain, color or temperature change, prior ulceration, amputation, angioplasty or bypass, tobacco exposure, kidney disease, vision difficulty, footwear habits, and ability to inspect feet.

Examine skin between toes, plantar surfaces, heels, nails, calluses, fissures, deformities, edema, pulses, capillary refill, dependent rubor or elevation pallor when appropriate, and footwear. Assess loss of protective sensation with a 10-g monofilament or an accepted alternative plus an additional neurologic modality as clinically indicated. Document what the patient can feel and where. A monofilament result is not a box to check; it changes ulcer-prevention intensity and follow-up frequency.

Part 3 — Ulcer Assessment: Describe What You See, Then Ask Why It Is There

For every ulcer, document site, size, depth, base tissue, callus, undermining, tunneling, drainage, odor, periwound erythema, warmth, edema, pain, necrosis, exposed tendon or bone, and whether it can be probed safely by a trained clinician. Assess vascular status and offloading needs. A plantar metatarsal ulcer under callus suggests pressure and neuropathy; a distal or lateral lesion with diminished pulses may signal ischemia; a new hot swollen midfoot with little pain may raise concern for Charcot neuroarthropathy.

Infection is diagnosed clinically from local or systemic inflammation, not from a swab alone. All chronic wounds are colonized. Purulence, spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness when sensation is intact, induration, lymphangitis, systemic signs, or unexplained metabolic deterioration can support infection. A wound culture without clinical infection should not automatically trigger antibiotics. Conversely, absence of fever does not make a diabetic foot infection benign.

Part 4 — PAD and Perfusion Change Every Decision

Peripheral artery disease can coexist with neuropathy and infection. Ask about exertional calf discomfort, rest pain, nonhealing wounds, color change, prior vascular procedures, and tobacco exposure; examine pulses and skin findings. Do not assume a warm-looking diabetic foot has adequate arterial flow, and do not use a palpable pulse alone to exclude disease. Abnormal perfusion, gangrene, nonhealing ulceration, ischemic pain, or tissue loss requires vascular assessment. Revascularization decisions are specialist decisions, but timely recognition is a primary-care responsibility.

Pressure relief without perfusion evaluation can fail; antibiotics without drainage or blood supply can fail; glucose optimization alone cannot heal a foot that remains under pressure and ischemic. Limb preservation requires integration.

Part 5 — Infection, Osteomyelitis, and the Urgency Ladder

Classify severity clinically. A severe infection, systemic illness, rapidly progressive inflammation, deep abscess, necrosis, gangrene, critical ischemia, gas, or suspected compartmental spread requires emergency and often surgical or hospital-based care. Moderate infection with key comorbidities may also need admission or expedited specialty management. If bone infection is suspected, initial evaluation commonly integrates examination, probe-to-bone assessment by an experienced clinician, plain radiographs, and inflammatory markers when the question is uncertain; advanced imaging and specialist input may be needed.

Purulent collections, necrotic tissue, deep abscess, gangrene, or concern for ischemia are not outpatient antibiotic-only problems. Antimicrobial selection, route, and duration depend on severity, likely or documented organisms, renal function, allergies, interactions, cultures from appropriate specimens, vascular supply, source control, and local guidance. The FNP coordinates these decisions; they are not made from a superficial wound swab alone.

Part 6 — Charcot Neuroarthropathy: A Limb-Saving Recognition

Consider acute Charcot neuroarthropathy in a patient with neuropathy who has a warm, swollen, red foot or ankle, often after minor trauma and sometimes with surprisingly little pain. It can mimic cellulitis, gout, sprain, or deep venous thrombosis. Continued weight bearing can collapse the foot architecture and create future ulceration. Prompt immobilization or offloading and urgent foot-specialist assessment are time-sensitive when Charcot is suspected; do not reassure a neuropathic patient solely because radiographs are initially unrevealing.

Part 7 — Offloading, Wound Care, and Patient Capacity

Offloading is a therapeutic intervention, not an optional lifestyle suggestion. The appropriate method depends on ulcer location, infection, ischemia, balance, fall risk, mobility, home support, and specialist direction. Wound dressing choice and debridement require assessment of tissue, exudate, perfusion, infection, and patient ability to perform care. Involve podiatry or wound specialists early when ulcers are deep, recurrent, ischemic, infected, or not healing as expected.

Ask who will inspect the foot, change the dressing, arrange transportation, obtain supplies, and call if the wound changes. A plan that ignores vision limitations, unstable housing, cost, work demands, or mobility may be medically correct and clinically ineffective.

Part 8 — Longitudinal Prevention

Teach daily inspection of soles and between toes, avoidance of barefoot walking, well-fitting protective footwear, prompt reporting of blisters or breaks in skin, skin hydration that avoids excessive moisture between toes, nail and callus care by appropriate clinicians, tobacco cessation support, and regular foot follow-up. Patients with sensory loss or prior ulcer need every-visit inspection and a clear specialty surveillance plan. Glycemic, blood-pressure, lipid, kidney, and vascular risk management remain part of foot preservation.

Part 9 — FNP Case: The Painless Plantar Ulcer

A patient with type 2 diabetes and numb feet discovers a callused plantar ulcer only after seeing drainage on a sock. There is minimal pain. The FNP measures and describes the wound, assesses sensation and pulses, looks for infection and deformity, arranges offloading and foot-care referral, and explains that lack of pain does not mean lack of danger. Follow-up is scheduled, not left to patient initiative alone.

Part 10 — FNP Case: The Red Hot Foot

A patient with longstanding neuropathy develops unilateral foot warmth, swelling, and redness after stepping off a curb. They report little pain, have no clear skin break, and have intact overall appearance. The FNP considers Charcot alongside infection and vascular concerns, limits weight bearing, and arranges urgent specialist evaluation rather than treating presumed cellulitis alone.

Part 11 — FNP Case: Ulcer With Fever and Dusky Toes

A patient with a chronic ulcer has new fever, spreading erythema, foul drainage, dusky toes, and weak pulses. This is not a routine wound check. The FNP recognizes combined infection and perfusion risk, arranges emergency evaluation with surgical and vascular capability, and communicates the wound history, diabetes status, antibiotics, allergies, and exam findings during transfer.

FNP High-Yield Framework: FOOT

  1. F — Find risk: sensory loss, PAD, deformity, prior ulcer or amputation, kidney disease, smoking, and ability to self-care.
  2. O — Observe the whole foot: skin, nails, callus, ulcer depth, drainage, pressure points, pulses, shoes, and gait.
  3. O — Offload and optimize: reduce pressure, coordinate wound care, support glycemic and vascular health, and remove practical barriers.
  4. T — Triage threat: infection severity, ischemia, gangrene, deep collection, osteomyelitis, Charcot, or systemic illness determine urgency.

Take-Home Summary

Limb preservation begins before ulceration and depends on identifying neuropathy, pressure, perfusion, and social barriers. In a diabetic foot ulcer, assess the whole system: wound, infection, bone, blood flow, offloading, function, and follow-up. A painless lesion can be serious, colonization is not infection, and antibiotics cannot replace source control, offloading, or revascularization when those are needed.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace in-person foot assessment, wound-care expertise, vascular or surgical consultation, current diabetes-foot guidelines, or emergency care. Fever, rapidly spreading infection, gangrene, ischemic change, deep tissue exposure, inability to bear weight with a hot swollen neuropathic foot, or systemic illness requires urgent evaluation.
